rows.evidence: Q1: Conditions and Methodology / Results - author's own 2007 data from 10 Watermark tensiometer nodes at 12 and 24 inch depths in a 4.4 acre Napa vineyard, correlated with 43 pressure-chamber leaf water potential points (Fig. 3). Q2: Results and Discussion - soil tension at 24 inch depth correlated with midday leaf water potential (R2 0.42); vineyard section reports 2007 yield of 3.97 t/acre (record, up from 1.81) and Brix peaking at 26.5-28; author states the general success of 2007 in yield and ripeness supports the SWT-based modified deficit irrigation, though indirectly. Q4: Results - leaf water potential (vine stress, the intermediate between soil tension and fruit quality) was measured with a pressure chamber on the same vines as the sensors and used to set the soil moisture target at 24 inches. Q7: Abstract and Results - author states that correlation with vine water status occurs only when sampled sufficiently (2-3 sites per acre) and at appropriate depth (24 inch, none at 12 inch); minimum 2 h irrigation duration needed because of 30 min line-pressure transients. Q8: Results - author states the yield/ripeness support is indirect because many confounding factors affect yield; outliers from an adjacent old vine and open-connection readings were removed; single vineyard, single season.
rows.notes: Evidence on crop production is observational: one vineyard, one season, no control treatment; yield and Brix are reported but not experimentally linked to the sensors. Q2 is answered yes with reservation because the study does report its own yield/quality outcome under SWT-managed irrigation and an SWT-leaf water potential correlation. Q6 answered no because the 4.4 acre vineyard functions as a single field despite being divided into irrigation blocks. Q9: only R2 reported, no dispersion measure. The review's context mentions a 150 kPa criterion at 60 cm; the study itself states a -13 bar leaf water potential threshold and does not name a 150 kPa value.

rows.evidence: Q1: Conditions and Methodology / Results - author's own 2007 soil tension data from 10 wireless Watermark nodes and own pressure-chamber measurements. Q2: Irrigation Paradigm and Results - 2007 irrigation totalled 34 gal/vine, a 26% reduction from 46 gal/vine in 2006, under the soil-moisture-based modified deficit irrigation; irrigation durations and intervals were set from the 24 inch sensor drying times and irrigation was delayed until a stress threshold; author states the reduced water use supports the approach, though indirectly. Q4: Results - soil tension at 24 inches (drying rate, wetting delay between 12 and 24 inches) and leaf water potential were measured and used to set irrigation intervals and the delayed start, the mechanism by which water was saved. Q7: Abstract and Results - author states sufficient sampling density and appropriate sensor depth (24 inch, not 12 inch) are needed for soil tension to track vine status; intervals were constrained by available water supply and a 2 h minimum duration due to line transients. Q8: Results and Irrigation Paradigm - author notes many confounding factors and that support is indirect; 2007 rainfall (16 inch) was far below 2006 (40 inch), and irrigation start was deliberately delayed in response to the dry winter.
rows.notes: The water saving is a year-to-year comparison on one vineyard with no control and confounded by a much drier winter and a deliberately delayed irrigation start; the study does not isolate the sensor contribution. Q2 answered yes with reservation because the reduced water use is reported as the study's own outcome of SWT-managed irrigation. Q6 no: single small vineyard. Q9: no dispersion measure for the water-use figures.

notes: Study is a single-vineyard practitioner case report (one season of correlation data, 10 monitoring sites, 43 data points). Text appears complete. Figures 2 and 3 partly rendered as text but their content is described in the body.
